bib.title: Python Data Science Handbook, Chapter 4: Visualization with Matplotlib

question: How do you build, annotate and style statistical and scientific plots in Python with Matplotlib, Basemap and Seaborn?
contributions: Tutorial coverage of Matplotlib 1.x/early-2.0-era plotting: line, scatter, error, density, legends, colorbars, subplots, annotation, ticks, styles, 3D, Basemap, Seaborn

results.claim: plt.plot is noticeably more efficient than plt.scatter once a dataset passes a few thousand points, because scatter builds each point separately.
Choose uniformly-bright colormaps: jet (default before Matplotlib 2.0) has uneven luminance; viridis (default as of 2.0) is built for even brightness and survives grayscale printing.

limits: Written for Matplotlib ~1.5 / pre-2.0 (author says 2.0 'will include a new default stylesheet'); version references in the text: styles need >=1.5, style module added in 1.4 (Aug 2014), jet default before 2.0, viridis default as of 2.0.
Author concedes Matplotlib feels 'clunky and old-fashioned' and expects the library list to be 'out of date as soon as it is published'; Basemap 'feels a bit clunky'.
No timings or benchmarks: the plot vs scatter efficiency claim is unmeasured.

READER NOTE (from my own knowledge, not the source): many calls in the chapter no longer work in current releases: hist(normed=True) -> density=True; plt.axes(axisbg=) -> facecolor=; sklearn.gaussian_process.GaussianProcess -> GaussianProcessRegressor; plt.cm.get_cmap -> matplotlib.colormaps[...] / plt.get_cmap; style names 'seaborn-whitegrid' etc. -> 'seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid'; pd.datetime and pd.datetools removed; sns.distplot/factorplot/pairplot(size=)/kdeplot(shade=) deprecated or renamed (histplot/displot, catplot, height=, fill=); positional args to sns.jointplot/violinplot/lmplot now need keywords; Basemap is deprecated in favour of Cartopy; plt.IndexFormatter removed; plt.axis(aspect='image') is a bug (should be ax.set_aspect or plt.axis('image')). Verify against current docs before teaching.
practices: Use plt.show() once per script, at the end; in IPython use %matplotlib, in notebooks %matplotlib inline or notebook (p.219-220).
Prefer the object-oriented interface (fig, ax = plt.subplots) once plots get complicated; the stateful pyplot interface makes returning to an earlier panel clumsy (p.222-223).
In OO code use ax.set(xlim=..., ylim=..., xlabel=..., ylabel=..., title=...) rather than separate set_* calls (p.232).
For large datasets prefer plt.plot over plt.scatter (p.237).
Draw continuous uncertainty with plt.fill_between and a low alpha instead of thousands of errorbars; lighten errorbars versus points in crowded plots (p.239-240).
For smooth 2D grids use plt.imshow with extent= and origin='lower' rather than very many contour levels (p.243).
Overplot histograms with histtype='stepfilled' and alpha for comparing distributions (p.246).
Label only the plot elements you want in the legend via label=; fake size legends by scattering empty lists with labels; add a second legend with ax.add_artist (p.252-254).
Avoid jet; use sequential maps (viridis, cubehelix) for ordered data and divergent maps (RdBu) for deviations from a centre, noting divergent sign information is lost in grayscale (p.257-259).
Clip colour limits with plt.clim and extend='both' when outliers swamp the scale; use plt.cm.get_cmap(name, N) for discrete colorbars (p.259-260).
Use plt.subplots(sharex=, sharey=) for grids and plt.GridSpec for irregular layouts such as marginal histograms (p.265-267).
Use annotate rather than plt.arrow, and anchor text with transAxes/transFigure when it should not move with data limits (p.270-273).
Hide ticks with NullLocator/NullFormatter for image grids; use MaxNLocator to declutter small subplots; FuncFormatter for custom labels (p.277-281).
Set defaults once via rcParams or stylesheets; use `with plt.style.context(name)` for temporary styles; use the grayscale style for print (p.285-289).
Start Basemap at low resolution and raise it only as needed (p.306-307).
Use Seaborn for statistical plots, but remember its output is Matplotlib so tick tweaks still apply (p.311, 326).
Check subgroup sizes before reading patterns in violin plots (7 runners over 80, p.329).

terms.definition: an instance of plt.Figure; a single container that contains all the objects representing axes, graphics, text, and labels
an instance of plt.Axes; a bounding box with ticks and labels, which will eventually contain the plot elements that make up our visualization
stateful pyplot interface that keeps track of the current figure and axes, reachable by plt.gcf() and plt.gca()
plotting functions are methods of explicit Figure and Axes objects rather than an active figure or axes
one continuous sequence of colors / two distinct colors showing positive and negative deviations from a mean / colors mixed with no particular sequence
coordinate systems for data, axes fraction and figure fraction used to anchor text
locators set tick positions and formatters set tick labels on each axis
runtime configuration holding default styles for every plot element; stylesheets are .mplstyle files formatted like .matplotlibrc
1 - 2*split_sec/final_sec; below zero means a negative split (faster second half)
